Celebrate bold ideas, but demand precision: correct p5.js API usage, real math, and reasoning about why a visual choice works. Ask 'what would happen if you changed this parameter?' constantly.

disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral — not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

choices: Call background() at the start of draw() to clear the canvas each frame
Draw fewer circles
Use a faster computer
Call noLoop()
scenarios.hint: What happens to last frame's pixels if nothing erases them — bug or feature?
scenarios.prompt: The artist wants a single clean circle following the mouse, but gets a smeared trail. Fix?
scenarios.situation: A sketch draws an ellipse at the mouse position every frame — but old ellipses never disappear.
scenarios.title: The smearing circle
scenarios.why: Without background() at the top of draw(), each frame paints over the last — the 'trail' effect. Calling background() clears the canvas every frame for clean animation. (Trails are also a beloved technique — achieved deliberately with a translucent background fill — but here they're the bug.)

choices: rect() is broken in this version
The canvas is too small
rect() draws from the corner by default (rectMode(CORNER)), and y grows downward — the rectangle extends right and down from (100, 100)
You must call stroke() first
scenarios.hint: What do the four numbers to rect() mean by default — and which corner do they start from?
scenarios.prompt: Why isn't the rectangle centered at (100, 100)?
scenarios.situation: An artist expects rect(100, 100, 60, 40) to center a rectangle at (100, 100), but it appears offset down and right.
scenarios.title: The off-center rectangle
scenarios.why: Default rectMode(CORNER): the first two args are the top-left corner, and with y growing downward the rect extends right and down from (100, 100). For centering, call rectMode(CENTER) once in setup(). The coordinate system (origin top-left, y down) is the source of half of all beginner layout bugs.

choices: p5.js has a style cache bug
Every fill() after the red one needs push()/pop() around the red shape to contain the style change
You can't use more than one fill per frame
Call background() between shapes
scenarios.hint: Drawing state (fill, stroke) persists until changed — how do you sandbox a temporary change?
scenarios.prompt: The third shape renders blue instead of gray. What's wrong?
scenarios.situation: After drawing a red ellipse and a blue rect, a third shape meant to be gray renders blue.
scenarios.title: The leaking fill
scenarios.why: fill() sets persistent drawing state — everything after fill(0,0,255) stays blue until changed. Wrap the blue rect in push()/pop() to sandbox its style, or set fill() again before the third shape. push()/pop() save and restore both styles and transformations; forgetting pop() is the classic state-leak.

choices: fill(180, 80, 90): hue 180 (cyan), saturation 80%, brightness 90%
fill(180, 80, 90): red 180, green 80, blue 90
HSB mode doesn't change fill()
The values are out of range and will error
scenarios.hint: colorMode(HSB, 360, 100, 100) redefines what the three numbers mean — what does 180 mean on a 360-degree wheel?
scenarios.prompt: What color does fill(180, 80, 90) produce?
scenarios.situation: After colorMode(HSB, 360, 100, 100), an artist writes fill(180, 80, 90).
scenarios.title: The HSB fill
scenarios.why: Hue 180° on the color wheel is cyan, at 80% saturation and 90% brightness. HSB separates 'which color' (hue) from 'how intense' (saturation) and 'how bright' — which is why generative artists love it: sweep the hue for rainbows, fix saturation/brightness for harmony. Forgetting colorMode is active is a classic source of 'wrong color' bugs.

choices: Draw everything twice
Use createGraphics() for an offscreen buffer: compose the static layer once, then image() it each frame
Take a screenshot and load it
It's impossible; everything must redraw
evidence: // 2000 static stars + 50 moving ships; stars redrawn every frame: 12 fps
scenarios.hint: If the stars never change, why pay to redraw them 60 times a second?
scenarios.prompt: How do you hit 60 fps?
scenarios.situation: 2000 static stars plus 50 moving ships: redrawing everything each frame runs at 12 fps.
scenarios.title: The static starfield
scenarios.why: Render the static stars once into an offscreen buffer (let pg = createGraphics(w, h)), then image(pg, 0, 0) each frame and draw only the 50 ships dynamically. Layering static content into buffers is the fundamental performance pattern in creative coding — separate what changes from what doesn't.

choices: The canvas can't change size after setup
Implement windowResized() { resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight); } and make layout relative
Reload the page on resize
Use fixed pixel positions everywhere
evidence:
function setup() { createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight); }
// layout uses absolute pixels; breaks on resize
scenarios.hint: p5.js has an event for exactly this — what should it do besides resizing?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the sketch survive window resizes?
scenarios.situation: A fullscreen sketch breaks its layout when the browser window resizes.
scenarios.title: The resize handler
scenarios.why: Define windowResized() to call resizeCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight) and recompute any layout cached from the old size. Robust sketches derive positions from width/height (fractions, not absolute pixels) so any canvas size works. Absolute-pixel layouts are the reason 'it worked on my monitor' is a meme.

choices: Increment x by a fixed amount each frame; frameCount gives you a free clock
Use random() for x each frame
Move x only when the mouse moves
x can't animate without a library
scenarios.hint: draw() already runs on a clock — what variable counts the ticks?
scenarios.prompt: How do you glide the circle across the screen?
scenarios.situation: A circle should glide smoothly left to right, looping forever.
scenarios.title: The gliding circle
scenarios.why: x = (frameCount * 2) % width: frameCount is a free frame clock, and modulo wraps it. Fixed per-frame increments are the simplest motion; the modulo makes it loop. (For frame-rate independence you'd use deltaTime — but for a first sketch, frameCount is the idiom.)

choices: random() each frame: jumpy and discontinuous
noise(): smooth Perlin noise that wanders organically; advance the noise offset slowly
sin() with a huge frequency
Hardcode positions
evidence: // want: a firefly that drifts organically
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between white noise and Perlin noise over time?
scenarios.prompt: Which function gives the firefly organic drift?
scenarios.situation: A firefly should wander smoothly, not teleport or march in a perfect sine wave.
scenarios.title: The firefly drift
scenarios.why: noise(t) returns smooth Perlin noise — nearby inputs give nearby outputs, so advancing t slowly yields wandering, organic paths. random() jumps discontinuously every call; sin() is too regular. noise() with slowly-advancing offsets (optionally separate offsets per axis) is the signature move of generative motion.

choices: Set x directly to the target; snapping is fine
Move x by a fixed 5 pixels per frame toward the target
x = lerp(x, targetX, 0.05): exponential easing that slows as it approaches
Use random() to jitter toward the target
evidence: // camera should glide toward the mouse, slowing as it arrives
scenarios.hint: What happens to the remaining distance each frame if you always cover 5% of it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you ease the camera toward the mouse?
scenarios.situation: A camera should glide toward the mouse position, decelerating as it arrives.
scenarios.title: The easing camera
scenarios.why: lerp(x, target, 0.05) moves 5% of the remaining distance per frame — fast at first, then asymptotically settling. This exponential ease-out is the most-used motion feel in creative coding (and UI animation). Fixed steps overshoot or crawl; lerp gives the buttery deceleration for free.

choices: Reverse velocity when the ball crosses an edge: if (x > width - r || x < r) vx *= -1
Teleport the ball to the center on hit
Stop the ball at the edge
Delete and respawn the ball
evidence:
let x, y, vx, vy;
// ball should bounce around the canvas forever
scenarios.hint: A bounce is a reflection — what happens to the velocity component perpendicular to the wall?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the ball bounce off the walls?
scenarios.situation: A ball with velocity (vx, vy) should bounce around the canvas forever.
scenarios.title: The bouncing ball
scenarios.why: When the ball's edge crosses a wall, flip the perpendicular velocity component (vx *= -1 for side walls). Account for the radius (x > width - r) so it bounces visually at the edge, not past it. Velocity + boundary reflection is the seed of every physics sketch — gravity, friction, and springs all layer onto this pattern.

choices: if (frameCount == 600) x = 0;
x = (x + speed) % width — modulo wraps the position
Manually detect the edge with a long if-chain
Restart the sketch with location.reload()
evidence: // particle stream should flow right and wrap around seamlessly
scenarios.hint: What arithmetic operation maps any growing number back into [0, width)?
scenarios.prompt: How do you loop the stream seamlessly?
scenarios.situation: Particles flow rightward and should wrap around the left edge seamlessly.
scenarios.title: The seamless wrap
scenarios.why: x = (x + speed) % width wraps any position back into [0, width) — the particle exits right and re-enters left with no pop. Modulo is the looping primitive: it also drives walk cycles, phase wrapping, and tiling. (For perfect GIF loops, make sure the motion period divides the frame count.)

choices: Fixed increments are fine; all screens are 60 fps
Count frames and assume 60 per second
Scale motion by deltaTime (milliseconds since last frame) so speed is real-time regardless of frame rate
Cap the frame rate with frameRate(30) and hope
evidence: x += 3;  // 60fps laptop: smooth. 120Hz display: double speed. Old phone: half speed.
scenarios.hint: If a frame takes twice as long, the object should travel twice as far that frame — what do you multiply by?
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep motion speed consistent across displays?
scenarios.situation: x += 3 per frame runs double-speed on 120Hz displays and half-speed on struggling phones.
scenarios.title: The frame-rate trap
scenarios.why: Multiply by deltaTime (ms since last frame): x += speed * (deltaTime / 1000) moves in real seconds, not frames. Frame-counted motion ties your artwork's timing to the viewer's hardware — deltaTime decouples them. This is the difference between a sketch and a robust piece.

choices: Nothing can be reproduced; that's the beauty of it
Set randomSeed() / noiseSeed() before generating; same seed replays the piece exactly
Screenshot every run
Avoid random() entirely
evidence: // collector wants to re-mint the exact piece they saw
scenarios.hint: Pseudorandom generators are deterministic — what single value determines the whole sequence?
scenarios.prompt: A collector wants the exact piece they saw re-generated. How?
scenarios.situation: A generative piece uses random() heavily; a collector wants to re-mint the precise variation they previewed.
scenarios.title: The seed as edition
scenarios.why: randomSeed(s) makes the pseudorandom sequence deterministic — same seed, same artwork, every time. The seed becomes the edition number: share it and anyone can re-render the identical piece. This is how generative art platforms (Art Blocks-style) work: the token's seed IS the artwork's DNA.

choices: Perfectly uniform grid; regularity is elegance
Nested loops with noise()-driven variation in size, rotation, and color — controlled irregularity
Place everything with random() and hope
One giant shape in the center
evidence: // 20x20 grid of squares looks dead and mechanical
scenarios.hint: Nature is neither uniform nor chaotic — what sits between a grid and confetti?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the grid feel alive?
scenarios.situation: A 20×20 grid of identical squares looks dead.
scenarios.title: The living grid
scenarios.why: Drive per-cell parameters with noise(): size = base + noise(x*0.1, y*0.1) * range, slight rotations, hue shifts. Smooth noise gives coherent variation — neighbors relate, nothing repeats mechanically, nothing dissolves into chaos. The grid-plus-noise pattern is the workhorse of generative composition: order as a scaffold, noise as the life.

choices: Copy-paste the branch code 8 levels deep
A recursive function: drawBranch(len) draws a segment, then calls itself twice at smaller lengths and rotated angles
Draw one branch and mirror it with scale(-1, 1)
Recursion can't draw trees
evidence: // want: a branching tree, 8 levels deep
scenarios.hint: A branch looks like a small tree — how do you express 'a tree is branches that end in smaller trees'?
scenarios.prompt: How do you draw the tree?
scenarios.situation: You want a branching tree, 8 levels deep, with natural-looking irregularity.
scenarios.title: The recursive tree
scenarios.why: function branch(len) { line(0,0,0,-len); translate(0,-len); rotate(a); branch(len*0.67); rotate(-2a); branch(len*0.67); } with a base case at small len. Recursion expresses self-similarity directly: each branch is a smaller tree. Add noise() to angles and length ratios for organic feel. Base case required — infinite recursion is a stack overflow, not a tree.

choices: Give each particle position + velocity, update with simple rules (attraction, repulsion, damping), and let the swarm emerge
Hand-animate 500 particles
One particle is enough; systems don't scale
Hardcode every trajectory
evidence: // want: 500 particles that swirl like a murmuration
scenarios.hint: Nobody choreographs a flock — what three local rules produce flocking?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get 500 particles to move like a murmuration?
scenarios.situation: You want a swirling, flocking particle system — not 500 hand-animated dots.
scenarios.title: The murmuration
scenarios.why: Particles with position + velocity following local rules (cohere toward neighbors, separate when crowded, align direction, plus damping) produce flocking nobody explicitly programmed — emergence. You design the rules, the system designs the motion. This is the generative mindset: author the system, curate the output.

choices: More code always means more interesting output
Constrain the parameter space tightly, then explore it systematically (grid search the seeds/params)
Only ever run it once
Complexity comes from large file sizes
evidence: // 40 parameters; every run looks either boring or broken
scenarios.hint: With 40 free parameters, what fraction of the space is actually good — and how do you find it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you find the good region of a huge parameter space?
scenarios.situation: 40 parameters; most runs are boring or broken; occasionally one is magic.
scenarios.title: The parameter desert
scenarios.why: Constrain ruthlessly (fewer, well-ranged parameters), then explore systematically: render contact sheets across seeds and key params, and keep what sings. Generative art is search — the artist's taste is the fitness function. Forty unconstrained parameters is a desert; eight tuned ones with good ranges is a garden.

choices: Export at screen resolution; it's fine
Render at high resolution with pixelDensity() / large offscreen buffers, using fixed seeds so the export matches the preview
Trace it by hand
Screenshots are the professional standard
evidence: Gallery wants a 48-inch print of the piece. Screen preview: 800px.
scenarios.hint: The piece is code, not pixels — what does that imply about resolution?
scenarios.prompt: How do you deliver a 48-inch print from an 800px preview?
scenarios.situation: A gallery wants a large-format print of your generative piece.
scenarios.title: The gallery export
scenarios.why: Re-render from the same seed at print resolution: pixelDensity(4), or a large createGraphics buffer, or scale all units. Because the artwork is a deterministic function of (seed, params), resolution is just a render setting — the unique advantage of code art over raster painting. Fixed seeds make the export match the approved preview exactly.

choices: if (mouseX > 0) fill(red);
Map it: let hue = map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360); — full sweep across the canvas
Use mouseX directly as the hue
Mouse can't drive color smoothly
evidence: // want: moving the mouse left-right sweeps the background through the rainbow
scenarios.hint: mouseX lives in [0, width]; hue wants [0, 360] — what function translates ranges?
scenarios.prompt: How do you sweep hue with the mouse?
scenarios.situation: Moving the mouse left to right should sweep the background through the full rainbow.
scenarios.title: The rainbow mouse
scenarios.why: map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360) translates the mouse range into hue degrees — left edge red, right edge back to red. map() is the universal adapter between input ranges and visual ranges. Direct use of mouseX as hue only works if width happens to be 360.

choices: They're identical; use either
mousePressed() fires once per click (event); checking mouseIsPressed in draw() is true for every frame the button is held
mouseIsPressed is deprecated
Events don't work in p5.js
evidence: // want: each click spawns ONE firework
scenarios.hint: One fires on the transition, the other reports the state — which one counts clicks?
scenarios.prompt: Each click should spawn exactly one firework. Which approach?
scenarios.situation: Checking mouseIsPressed inside draw() spawns dozens of fireworks per click.
scenarios.title: The firework spam
scenarios.why: mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click). Events for discrete actions (spawn, toggle), polling for continuous ones (dragging, holding). Mixing them up is the classic interaction bug.

choices: Poll keyIsPressed in draw() for everything
Use keyPressed() for discrete actions and check key / keyCode for which key; poll in draw() only for held-key movement
Keyboard input isn't supported
One key per sketch maximum
evidence: // spacebar: pause. Arrow keys: held down to steer.
scenarios.hint: Same split as the mouse: which action is discrete (pause) and which is continuous (steering)?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle spacebar-to-pause plus arrow-key steering?
scenarios.situation: Spacebar should toggle pause; held arrow keys should steer continuously.
scenarios.title: The keyboard split
scenarios.why: keyPressed() with (key === ' ') toggles pause once per press — discrete. Arrow steering polls keyIsDown(LEFT_ARROW) in draw() — continuous. Same event/state split as the mouse. Note key holds the character, keyCode the physical key (arrows, shift) — use keyCode for arrows.

choices: Hardcode values; sliders are for amateurs
createSlider() for live parameters: bind hue, speed, and complexity to sliders and read .value() in draw()
Rebuild the sketch for each variation
Sliders can't update a running sketch
evidence: // artist wants to perform the piece live, tuning 3 parameters
scenarios.hint: p5.js ships DOM elements for this — what creates a draggable control in one line?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the piece performable live?
scenarios.situation: An artist wants to perform the piece, tuning hue, speed, and complexity in real time.
scenarios.title: The live sliders
scenarios.why: let hueSlider = createSlider(0, 360, 180); then hue = hueSlider.value() in draw(). Sliders turn parameters into instruments — the piece becomes performable, and tuning becomes play instead of edit-compile cycles. Expose the 3–5 parameters that matter; hide the rest.

choices: Touch works automatically with no code
Define touchStarted() (and touchMoved/touchEnded); also return false to prevent page scroll
Mobile browsers can't run p5.js
Use mousePressed only; it covers touch
evidence: // piece must work on phones at the gallery
scenarios.hint: Phones fire touch events, not mouse events — and the browser wants to scroll. What handles both?
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the interaction work on phones?
scenarios.situation: A gallery piece must run on visitors' phones.
scenarios.title: The touch gap
scenarios.why: Implement touchStarted()/touchMoved() alongside (or instead of) mouse handlers, and return false to stop the browser scrolling/zooming over your canvas. mousePressed sometimes fires on mobile, but unreliably — dedicated touch handlers are the robust path. Test on a real phone; simulators lie about touch.

choices: One giant draw() with flags everywhere
A state variable (e.g., mode = 'attract' | 'play' | 'rest') with a switch in draw() and transitions on events/timeout
Separate HTML pages per scene
States are overengineering
evidence: // installation: attract loop -> interactive play -> rest screen, cycling
scenarios.hint: Three behaviors, clean transitions — what pattern keeps them from tangling?
scenarios.prompt: How do you structure the installation's three modes?
scenarios.situation: An installation cycles: attract loop, interactive play, rest screen.
scenarios.title: The mode machine
scenarios.why: A mode variable with a switch in draw() — each case self-contained, transitions triggered by events or timers. States keep behaviors from tangling into flag spaghetti, and adding a fourth mode later is trivial. Almost every interactive installation is a small state machine wearing an art costume.

choices: Multiply the sensor value by 2 and hope
map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400): translate the 10-bit range into a radius range
Use the raw value as the radius
Sensors can't drive visuals
evidence: Sensor reads 0-1023. Want: circle radius 20-400 px.
scenarios.hint: map() takes five arguments — value, then the input range, then the output range. What are they here?
scenarios.prompt: How do you convert the sensor reading into a radius?
scenarios.situation: A 10-bit sensor (0–1023) should drive a circle's radius (20–400 px).
scenarios.title: The sensor mapping
scenarios.why: map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400) linearly translates ranges — the single most-used function in interactive art. It also clamps nothing by default (values outside map outside — constrain() if needed) and works in reverse (map(x, 0, 1023, 400, 20) inverts). Range translation is the whole job of physical computing.

choices: x = r * a; y = r * a;
x = cx + r * cos(a); y = cy + r * sin(a); — with a in radians
x = cx + a; y = cy + a;
Circles can't be parametric
evidence: // want: 12 dots evenly spaced on a circle of radius 150
scenarios.hint: A point on a circle is an angle plus a radius — how do sine and cosine split those into x and y?
scenarios.prompt: How do you place 12 dots evenly on a circle?
scenarios.situation: Twelve dots, evenly spaced, on a circle of radius 150 centered at (cx, cy).
scenarios.title: The polar layout
scenarios.why: For i in 0..11: a = i * TWO_PI / 12; x = cx + 150*cos(a); y = cy + 150*sin(a). Polar coordinates (angle, radius) are the natural language of circular layouts — orbits, radial menus, flower petals, clock faces. TWO_PI/12 spaces them evenly; cos/sin project onto x/y.

choices: rotate() takes degrees; the code is fine
Multiply by 100 to fix it
rotate() expects radians: rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) — 45 radians spins ~7 full turns
Use rotateX instead
evidence: rotate(45);  // expected: tilt 45 degrees. Got: wild spinning.
scenarios.hint: 45 of what? p5.js trig functions default to one angular unit — which?
scenarios.prompt: Why does rotate(45) spin wildly instead of tilting 45°?
scenarios.situation: rotate(45) was meant to tilt 45 degrees but produces wild spinning.
scenarios.title: The radian trap
scenarios.why: p5.js trig defaults to radians: 45 radians ≈ 7.16 full rotations. Fix with rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) in setup(). This is the most common math bug in creative coding — always check which unit a function expects before assuming degrees.

choices: lerpColor(colorA, colorB, t) with t swept 0→1 across the shape
Alternate fill() calls randomly
Use two canvases
Gradients are impossible in p5.js
evidence: // want: smooth vertical gradient from deep blue to warm orange
scenarios.hint: A gradient is just many small steps — what interpolates between two colors?
scenarios.prompt: How do you paint the gradient?
scenarios.situation: A smooth vertical gradient from deep blue to warm orange.
scenarios.title: The gradient blend
scenarios.why: Loop over rows: t = y / height; stroke(lerpColor(blue, orange, t)); line across. lerpColor interpolates every channel by t — the color twin of lerp(). In HSB mode the blend travels through hue space (often prettier); in RGB it can pass through muddy middles. Gradients are interpolation made visible.

choices: Check every pair with nested ifs on raw coordinates
dist(x1, y1, x2, y2) < threshold — Euclidean distance, one call
Estimate with x-distance only
Proximity can't be computed per frame
evidence: // 200 particles; nearby pairs should connect with lines
scenarios.hint: 'Nearby' is a distance — what function computes it directly?
scenarios.prompt: How do you find nearby particle pairs?
scenarios.situation: 200 particles; pairs closer than 60px should be connected with lines.
scenarios.title: The proximity lines
scenarios.why: if (dist(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y) < 60) line(...). dist() is Euclidean distance in one call — the basis of connection effects, repulsion, attraction, and collision. (At 200 particles, all-pairs is 20k checks/frame — fine; at 2000, you'd want spatial hashing. Know your n².)

choices: Place seeds randomly; nature is random
Use the golden angle 137.5°: each seed at angle i*137.5°, radius growing with sqrt(i) — optimal packing, zero overlap
Space them evenly at 180°
Packing doesn't matter visually
evidence: // want: a sunflower head of 500 seeds, perfectly packed
scenarios.hint: 137.5° is 360°/φ² — the most irrational turn. Why would irrationality pack best?
scenarios.prompt: How do you pack 500 seeds like a sunflower?
scenarios.situation: A sunflower head: 500 seeds, perfectly packed, no overlaps, no gaps.
scenarios.title: The golden angle
scenarios.why: Angle = i × 137.5°, radius = c × √i. The golden angle (360°/φ²) is the 'most irrational' turn, so no seed ever lines up behind another — optimal packing emerges from one multiplication. Radius grows with √i so area per seed stays constant. This is phyllotaxis: mathematics' most beautiful generative algorithm, running in every sunflower.

choices: Buy a faster laptop
Reduce per-frame work: fewer objects, noStroke() where possible, avoid allocations in draw(), use buffers for static layers
Increase frameRate(120)
Add more visual effects
evidence: 3000 particles with shadows and blur: 9 fps. Target: 60.
scenarios.hint: Profile the cost per particle — which operations are the most expensive per frame?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get from 9 fps to 60?
scenarios.situation: 3000 particles with per-particle shadows and blur run at 9 fps.
scenarios.title: The frame-rate rescue
scenarios.why: Kill the expensive per-frame ops first: shadows/blur are brutally costly — fake them with gradients or drop them. Then: fewer objects, noStroke(), no per-frame allocations (GC pauses), static layers into buffers. Creative-coding performance is almost always about doing less per frame, not faster hardware.

choices: Fixed 1920×1080 canvas; everyone has that
createCanvas(windowWidth, windowHeight), derive all layout from width/height, handle windowResized()
Detect the device brand and hardcode
One canvas size per visitor, chosen at random
evidence: Piece shown on phones, laptops, and a 4K gallery wall.

scenarios.why: Fullscreen canvas + relative layout (positions as fractions of width/height) + windowResized() handler. The piece becomes a function of the viewport, not a fixed image. Present from the code editor

lessons.title: Canvas & Drawing — Core concepts
concepts: draw() loop: without background() at the top of draw(), each frame paints over the last — the 'trail' effect. Render the static stars once into an offscreen buffer (let pg = createGraphics(w, h)), then image(pg, 0, 0) each frame and draw only the 50 ships dynamically.
background(): calling background() clears the canvas every frame for clean animation.
rectMode: default rectMode(CORNER): the first two args are the top-left corner, and with y growing downward the rect extends right and down from (100, 100).
Coordinate system: the coordinate system (origin top-left, y down) is the source of half of all beginner layout bugs.

push()/pop(): wrap the blue rect in push()/pop() to sandbox its style, or set fill() again before the third shape. push()/pop() save and restore both styles and transformations; forgetting pop() is the classic state-leak.
Drawing state: fill() sets persistent drawing state — everything after fill(0,0,255) stays blue until changed.

example.walkthrough: Hue 180° on the color wheel is cyan, at 80% saturation and 90% brightness. HSB separates 'which color' (hue) from 'how intense' (saturation) and 'how bright' — which is why generative artists love it: sweep the hue for rainbows, fix saturation/brightness for harmony. Forgetting colorMode is active is a classic source of 'wrong color' bugs.

pitfalls: Common trap: use createGraphics() for an offscreen buffer: compose the static layer once, then image() it each frame.
Common trap: HSB mode doesn't change fill().
Common trap: the canvas can't change size after setup.
Common trap: use fixed pixel positions everywhere.

lessons.title: Animation — Core concepts
concepts: frameCount: x = (frameCount * 2) % width: frameCount is a free frame clock, and modulo wraps it.
Motion basics: (For perfect GIF loops, make sure the motion period divides the frame count.). Fixed per-frame increments are the simplest motion; the modulo makes it loop.

noise(): noise(t) returns smooth Perlin noise — nearby inputs give nearby outputs, so advancing t slowly yields wandering, organic paths. random() jumps discontinuously every call; sin() is too regular. noise() with slowly-advancing offsets (optionally separate offsets per axis) is the signature move of generative motion.

Organic motion: this exponential ease-out is the most-used motion feel in creative coding (and UI animation). Frame-counted motion ties your artwork's timing to the viewer's hardware — deltaTime decouples them.
lerp(): lerp(x, target, 0.05) moves 5% of the remaining distance per frame — fast at first, then asymptotically settling.

example.code:
let x, y, vx, vy;
// ball should bounce around the canvas forever
example.walkthrough: When the ball's edge crosses a wall, flip the perpendicular velocity component (vx *= -1 for side walls). Account for the radius (x > width - r) so it bounces visually at the edge, not past it. Velocity + boundary reflection is the seed of every physics sketch — gravity, friction, and springs all layer onto this pattern.

pitfalls: Common trap: move x by a fixed 5 pixels per frame toward the target.
Common trap: cap the frame rate with frameRate(30) and hope.
Common trap: random() each frame: jumpy and discontinuous.
Common trap: set x directly to the target; snapping is fine.

lessons.title: Generative Systems — Core concepts
concepts: RandomSeed(s) makes the pseudorandom sequence deterministic — same seed, same artwork, every time.
Controlled variation: smooth noise gives coherent variation — neighbors relate, nothing repeats mechanically, nothing dissolves into chaos.
Recursion expresses self-similarity directly: each branch is a smaller tree.

example.code: // collector wants to re-mint the exact piece they saw
example.walkthrough: randomSeed(s) makes the pseudorandom sequence deterministic — same seed, same artwork, every time. The seed becomes the edition number: share it and anyone can re-render the identical piece. This is how generative art platforms (Art Blocks-style) work: the token's seed IS the artwork's DNA.

pitfalls: Common trap: render at high resolution with pixelDensity() / large offscreen buffers, using fixed seeds so the export matches the preview.
Common trap: one particle is enough; systems don't scale.
Common trap: set randomSeed() / noiseSeed() before generating; same seed replays the piece exactly.
Common trap: export at screen resolution; it's fine.

lessons.title: Interaction — Core concepts
concepts: map(): map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360) translates the mouse range into hue degrees — left edge red, right edge back to red. map() is the universal adapter between input ranges and visual ranges.

Mouse input: implement touchStarted()/touchMoved() alongside (or instead of) mouse handlers, and return false to stop the browser scrolling/zooming over your canvas. mousePressed sometimes fires on mobile, but unreliably — dedicated touch handlers are the robust path.
Event functions: mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click).

Polling vs events: events for discrete actions (spawn, toggle), polling for continuous ones (dragging, holding). A mode variable with a switch in draw() — each case self-contained, transitions triggered by events or timers.
KeyPressed() with (key === ' ') toggles pause once per press — discrete.
keyCode: note key holds the character, keyCode the physical key (arrows, shift) — use keyCode for arrows.

example.code: // artist wants to perform the piece live, tuning 3 parameters
example.walkthrough: let hueSlider = createSlider(0, 360, 180); then hue = hueSlider.value() in draw(). Sliders turn parameters into instruments — the piece becomes performable, and tuning becomes play instead of edit-compile cycles. Expose the 3–5 parameters that matter; hide the rest.

pitfalls: Common trap: createSlider() for live parameters: bind hue, speed, and complexity to sliders and read .value() in draw().
Common trap: use keyPressed() for discrete actions and check key / keyCode for which key; poll in draw() only for held-key movement.
Common trap: a state variable (e.g., mode = 'attract' | 'play' | 'rest') with a switch in draw() and transitions on events/timeout.
Common trap: map it: let hue = map(mouseX, 0, width, 0, 360);.

lessons.title: Math for Art — Core concepts
concepts: map(): map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400) linearly translates ranges — the single most-used function in interactive art.
Polar coordinates (angle, radius) are the natural language of circular layouts — orbits, radial menus, flower petals, clock faces.
Radians: fix with rotate(radians(45)) or angleMode(DEGREES) in setup().
lerpColor: loop over rows: t = y / height; stroke(lerpColor(blue, orange, t)); line across. lerpColor interpolates every channel by t — the color twin of lerp().
dist(): if (dist(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y) < 60) line(...). dist() is Euclidean distance in one call — the basis of connection effects, repulsion, attraction, and collision.

example.code: // want: 12 dots evenly spaced on a circle of radius 150
example.walkthrough: For i in 0..11: a = i * TWO_PI / 12; x = cx + 150*cos(a); y = cy + 150*sin(a). TWO_PI/12 spaces them evenly; cos/sin project onto x/y.

pitfalls: Common trap: use the golden angle 137.5°: each seed at angle i*137.5°, radius growing with sqrt(i).
Common trap: check every pair with nested ifs on raw coordinates.
Common trap: map(sensor, 0, 1023, 20, 400): translate the 10-bit range into a radius range.
Common trap: rotate() takes degrees; the code is fine.

lessons.title: Showcase — Core concepts
concepts: Performance: creative-coding performance is almost always about doing less per frame, not faster hardware. Present like a projectionist, not a programmer: the piece is the performance.
Responsive generative art is layout-as-function.
prefers-reduced-motion: check matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') and offer a calm alternative: static composition, slow drift, no flashing.

example.code: 3000 particles with shadows and blur: 9 fps. Target: 60.
example.walkthrough: Kill the expensive per-frame ops first: shadows/blur are brutally costly — fake them with gradients or drop them. Then: fewer objects, noStroke(), no per-frame allocations (GC pauses), static layers into buffers.

pitfalls: Common trap: add a prefers-reduced-motion check: offer a static or gentle mode when the user requests reduced motion.
Common trap: fullscreen presentation: fullscreen(true) on interaction, noCursor(), hide UI chrome.
Common trap: motion is the art; accessibility doesn't apply.
Common trap: read the code aloud as the presentation.

lessons.title: Creative Coding — Core concepts
concepts: The canvas is a bitmap with two sizes: the backing store (actual pixels) and the CSS box (logical pixels). Multiply the backing store by devicePixelRatio and scale the context, or high-DPI screens turn your art to mush.

Animate with requestAnimationFrame, not timers: it syncs to vsync, sleeps in background tabs, and hands you a timestamp — use the delta so motion speed is frame-rate independent across 60 Hz and 120 Hz displays.

Generative art is deterministic randomness: a seeded PRNG (like mulberry32) turns the seed into the artwork's identity — same seed, same piece, re-renderable at any size, shareable as a single number.

WebGL splits work by frequency: the vertex shader runs per vertex (geometry, transforms), the fragment shader runs per pixel (color, detail). High-frequency detail like noise belongs in the fragment stage.
Trails and feedback effects are exponential decay, not accumulation: fade the frame with a translucent background rect each tick instead of adding light forever, or the image clips to white.
GLSL precision is a portability concern: declare precision explicitly, request highp where noise/math needs it, and provide mediump fallbacks — mobile GPUs do not guarantee desktop defaults.

example.walkthrough: mulberry32 is a tiny, well-known seeded generator. Every call advances a deterministic sequence, so the entire composition derives from the initial seed — the prized output can be re-rendered exactly by reusing its seed.

pitfalls: Common trap: setting canvas.width/height via CSS only — the backing store stays 300×150 default and everything stretches blurry.
Common trap: assuming 16 ms per frame — on 120 Hz displays or throttled tabs your motion runs at the wrong speed; always use the rAF timestamp delta.
Common trap: Math.random() everywhere — the artwork can never be reproduced, versioned, or re-rendered at print resolution; seed your randomness.
Common trap: computing per-pixel detail in the vertex shader — 4 vertices cannot carry a noise field; that work belongs in the fragment shader.

evidence: Seed logged per render; favorite outputs reproducible from the log.

Hue 180° on the color wheel is cyan, at 80% saturation and 90% brightness. HSB separates 'which color' (hue) from 'how intense' (saturation) and 'how bright' — which is why generative artists love it: sweep the hue for rainbows, fix satu…
Event functions: mousePressed() is an event: it fires once per click. mouseIsPressed is state: true for every frame the button stays down (dozens of frames per click).

checklist: Set a 90-minute focused block; silence notifications and close unrelated tabs.
Warm up by re-reading yesterday's notes before starting new material.
Work every example by hand or in the sandbox — never just read them.
Write each key term and formula in your own words in a notebook.
After each domain, close the material and recite the core ideas aloud.
Redo the problems you missed until you can solve them cold.
Take a 10-minute break every 50 minutes — spaced effort beats cramming.
End the session by listing the three ideas you are least sure about, and drill those first next time.
Spend extra time on Canvas & Drawing: teach its core ideas back in plain language.
Re-derive the key Animation results from scratch without peeking.
